chapter: The Savoy band and the Swing era
title: Rejecting the "Father of Swing" title and firsts
summary: Carter rejects the title Father of Swing and discusses how interviewers press for firsts and neat answers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Right. Well, that's why people are interested in these things, and I think that -- you know -- that many fans and many writers like to say that your true role in the development of Swing and the background of Swing -- not in Swing itself necessarily, has been underestimated, and that is somehow regarded as a compliment to you; that you played a bigger role than you've been given credit for.
Well, as a matter of fact, I've been called the "Father of Swing". They could have been even less kind -- they could have said Grandfather!
Right. But you don't reject that title, do you? That doesn't bother you.
What do you mean -- the Father of Swing?
Yes, the Father of Swing.
Yes, I do reject it because I don't think it's properly applied to the person who may have made it, you know, created Swing. I certainly didn't.
But you couldn't say who did?
No, so therefore why should I accept such a title?
Well, I think what they mean is ...
That's just like Jelly Roll Morton; I claim I invented it.
Yes. Well, you see, your fans and the writers are not so hesitant about these things. Which is appropriate.
Uh huh.

You see, this becomes a big thing; people are always looking for the first time this happened, the first time that happened, and of course, people's lives are not worked out in such a way that they always know the first time something happened, when like, I asked you, when -- what was the first recording, what was the first trumpet solo, or what did you regard yourself, or when did you pick up the trumpet again after you had put it down and so on.
Yeah.

I mean, people are interested in these things, and if you take such statments and such dates in the appropriate way, I think that they are helpful as long as you don't place too much credence in what they propose to tell.
In the answers. Well, I mean, I'm always kind of baffled by the how, when and why situation, you know?
Yes ... yeah.
'Cause I don't really know.

Well, it often leads people to make up answers, or not only to make them up, but rather, to give certain stress to things which perhaps don't deserve that degree of stress, but it becomes an answer to a question and it sounds a lot more definite, then perhaps it really was.
Sometimes it provides an answer to a question just to get rid of it.
That's it ... yes.
Right.

That happens a great deal, too, and the writers and the interviewers in jazz have only themselves to blame for the fact that very often, a response is the only way to get rid of them, and get back to the stand, where they belong, while the owner is looking on.
Right.
